english_translation: I have saved a little money so that I can buy some other things tomorrow.

dialogue.shona: Ndachengeta mari shoma; kuti ndigozotenge zvimwe zvinhu mangwana.
dialogue.english: I have saved a little money so that I can buy some other things tomorrow.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndachengeta [ndachengeta] • mari [plural ri] • shoma [shoma] • kuti [that / so that] • ndigozotenge [ndigozotenge] • zvimwe [things mwe] • zvinhu [things nhu] • mangwana [tomorrow]

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Ndachengeta mari shoma; kuti ndigozotenge zvimwe zvinhu mangwana.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.title: Describing Nouns: Word Order in Shona
grammar_notes.content: In English, descriptive words like adjectives, possessives ('my', 'our'), demonstratives ('this', 'that'), and numbers come BEFORE the noun ('this big house', 'my two books'). In Shona, the noun always comes FIRST, and all descriptive words follow right after it! For example: 'nyama iyi' ('this meat'), 'mwana uyu' ('this child'), 'goho guru' ('a big harvest'), and 'makomo marefu' ('tall mountains').
grammar_notes.rule: Noun FIRST + Descriptor SECOND -> mota iyi (this car), mabhuku edu (our books), makomo marefu (tall mountains)

cultural_notes.title: Household Budgeting & Saving ('Kuchengeta Mari') for Market Days
cultural_notes.content: Careful household budgeting—setting aside small savings ('kuchengeta mari shoma') or participating in community savings clubs ('mukando' / 'marounds')—helps families purchase groceries and school supplies without strain.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new polite request into English: 'Chimbomirira zvishoma pamusuwo.'
options: Come inside the house and sit on the chair.
Return home early before the sun sets.
Take your books and put them in the bag.
Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Chimbomirira' = 'Wait a little / for a moment right now', 'zvishoma' = 'a little', 'pamusuwo' = 'at the door'.

active_exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'The girl is wearing a yellow hat and a blue dress'?
options: Musikana akapfeka ngowani yeyero nerokwe rebhuruu.
Mukomana akapfeka bhachi dema neshangu tsvuku.
Mbatya dzose dziri kuoma pamutambo panze.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Musikana akapfeka ngowani yeyero nerokwe rebhuruu.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Ngowani yeyero' = 'a yellow hat', and 'nerokwe rebhuruu' = 'and a blue dress'.
